statements.statement: A digital signal can represent three states: high, medium, and low.
statements.explanation: A digital signal has exactly two states: high or low, on or off, 1 or 0. There is no in-between or medium state. This binary nature is fundamental to how digital works.

statements.statement: A light switch is a good analogy for a digital signal because it is either fully on or fully off.
statements.explanation: A light switch clicks fully on or fully off, never halfway, just like a digital signal that is always in one of two distinct states with nothing in between.

statements.statement: Computers send and receive information using patterns of on/off pulses.
statements.explanation: Every piece of information a computer processes is built from simple on/off (1/0) pulses strung together in patterns. Complex data like text, images, and video are all encoded as sequences of these binary states.

statements.statement: A digital signal can be set to any voltage value between high and low.
statements.explanation: A digital signal has no in-between. It is either high or low; there are no intermediate values. This is the fundamental difference between digital and analog signals.
